analysis.one_liner: Lets workers take age discrimination claims to court even if they signed an arbitration agreement.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill letting workers sue over age discrimination cleared committee in May 2024 with no recorded dissent, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most large employers require new hires to sign agreements promising to settle any dispute in private arbitration, which also usually bans group lawsuits. This bill would make such agreements unenforceable for age discrimination claims, if the worker chooses to go to court. A judge, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies. The bill applied only going forward, to claims arising after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers age 40 and older who face age discrimination on the job. Instead of being funneled into private arbitration, where cases are decided one at a time with no appeal in most situations, they could file in court, join class or collective actions, and have their case heard publicly.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes predispute arbitration agreements and predispute joint-action waivers invalid and unenforceable for age discrimination disputes, at the election of the person alleging the discrimination or a class representative.
It covers all forms of age discrimination prohibited under federal, tribal, or state law against people 40 and older, including disparate treatment, disparate impact, harassment, and retaliation.
A court, not an arbitrator, decides whether the law applies and whether the arbitration agreement is enforceable, even if the contract says an arbitrator should make that call.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would lose their ability to keep age discrimination claims out of court and out of group lawsuits. Arbitration providers and the courts would also adjust, with more cases filed publicly.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it covers only age discrimination. Predispute arbitration agreements remain enforceable for discrimination claims based on sex, race, disability, and other grounds, so workers on those tracks get no new protection.

The choice runs one way: the worker may elect out of arbitration, but employers can no longer offer it for age claims. Workers who prefer arbitration's lower upfront cost and faster timeline would lose that option, and litigation is generally slower and more expensive to pursue, especially for a single case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but modest in scope. Arbitration agreements function as a lock: most workers sign them as a condition of employment without meaningful bargaining, and the joint-action waivers embedded in them prevent the group lawsuits that give age discrimination cases bargaining power. The trade-off is more cost and delay for individual workers who now go to court, and the bill does nothing for workers facing other kinds of discrimination. On balance it shifts power back toward older workers at a real but contained cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate's waiting list for floor action, but the Senate never took it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 14, 2023, by Senator Gillibrand with fourteen original cosponsors, including Republicans Lindsey Graham, Chuck Grassley, and Josh Hawley, and was referred to the Judiciary Committee.

On May 9, 2024, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and on May 16, 2024, it was reported and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 396.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a Senate floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and it never reached the House.
The bill would have applied only to claims arising on or after its date of enactment, so no existing arbitration agreement would have been affected retroactively.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who keep mandatory arbitration for age discrimination claims, and the arbitration industry that staffs those cases. Older workers gained nothing; the bill died without a vote despite clearing committee with bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee without amendment and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar.

for.name: Sens. Lindsey Graham, Chuck Grassley, and Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on May 9, 2024, with no recorded opposition.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was reported from committee and placed on the calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction: a Democrat sponsored it alongside at least three Senate Republicans among its fourteen original cosponsors, and the Judiciary Committee reported it favorably without amendment.

industries.note: Employers currently use pre-hire arbitration agreements to keep age discrimination claims out of court and block group lawsuits. The bill would remove that shield for age claims, exposing them to public court cases and class actions. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against the older workers who would gain a courtroom right.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employer-side arbitration defense practices
industries.note: Mandatory employment arbitration is a large fee-generating channel; removing age discrimination cases from it shrinks the market. Providers profit from agreements workers must sign to get a job, so their interest runs against the workers this bill would help.
